sections.text: Maurice Merleau-Ponty's connection to idealism has long been debated in philosophical circles. Although his phenomenology is rooted in embodied subjectivity—the idea that subjectivity, or the self, is always tied to and shaped by bodily experience—it challenges the standard assumptions of the idealist tradition. In Embodied Idealism, Berendzen tackles Merleau-Pontys transcendental idealism, grounded in embodiment, as presented in his early works. The book is divided into two parts: the first focuses on Merleau-Ponty's work before Phenomenology of Perception and the second on Phenomenology of Perception itself; I will consider the contributions and limitations of each in turn.

sections.heading: Part I: Idealism Before *Phenomenology of Perception*
sections.text:
Berendzen begins with a detailed historical and philosophical context for Merleau-Ponty's engagement with idealism. Merleau-Ponty's earliest critiques appear in The Structure of Behavior, where he confronts earlier iterations of idealism, especially the subjective idealism of Berkeley. While he challenges the notion that reality is determined solely by mind or consciousness, Merleau-Ponty does not simply dismiss the idea that mind helps shape reality. Instead, he emphasizes that perception cannot be reduced to abstract mental constructs: It is always situated in a physical, interactive environment.
On Berendzen's view, Merleau-Ponty highlights the body's vital role. Merleau-Ponty insists that perceiving the world involves a living, sensing being in dynamic contact with the things around it; thus, mind and world are not locked in a one-way relationship. The problem with pure subjective idealism, from his perspective, is its tendency to ignore or minimize the constitutive power of bodily engagement. Merleau-Ponty's initial move away from purely mentalistic theories sets the stage for his later exploration of transcendental idealism, now reoriented around lived, embodied perception.
Berendzen then examines Merleau-Ponty's idea of “expression” in The Structure of Behavior, wherein Merleau-Ponty distances himself from strict behaviorism. Behaviorism views human beings primarily as bundles of stimulus–response patterns, whereas Merleau-Ponty sees perception as a creative, embodied process. Some passages can appear to reduce perception to a chain of bodily actions, but Berendzen underscores that Merleau-Ponty's real aim is more subtle. Reality is encountered “through” the body, making idealism and realism intersect, because what we call “the real” emerges in the interplay between an active, perceiving subject and its environment.
The third chapter details Merleau-Ponty's negotiations with the legacy of Kant and Husserl, two philosophers who profoundly influenced him while also prompting him to depart from their more traditional formulations. Kant's conception of a transcendental subject that structures experience independent of embodiment became, for Merleau-Ponty, too detached from the real conditions of perception. Likewise, Husserl's transcendental phenomenology, though influential, appeared to Merleau-Ponty to over-rely on the reflective ego.
Berendzen shows how Merleau-Ponty works to revise these frameworks, forging a “relation-based” or “situated” transcendental idealism that acknowledges perception as an active, bodily engagement with the world. This not only breaks away from classical dualisms but also signals an emerging phenomenology of co-constitution: Mind and world interweave, each shaping the other. For Berendzen, Merleau-Ponty's early development thus heralds a new philosophical landscape, one that prizes dynamic, reciprocal relations over static categories of subject and object.

sections.heading: Part II: Idealism in *Phenomenology of Perception*
sections.text:
In Phenomenology of Perception, Merleau-Ponty both refutes the rigid Cartesian divide between mind and body and reconceptualizes the role of consciousness in constituting the real. While he does not deny the involvement of consciousness in shaping experience, he insists that consciousness is inherently relational and intertwined with bodily capacities. According to Berendzen, this view avoids both the extremes of pure intellectualism and a reductive neo-Kantian framework. Instead, Merleau-Ponty posits that perception is, prior to all explicit knowledge, serving as the soil from which concepts and judgments later grow.
Berendzen explores how Phenomenology of Perception transforms the notion of transcendental idealism by making the lived body central. Far from being simply another material object, the body is the origin of perception and action. Merleau-Ponty's “embodied idealism” holds that reality emerges through the relationship between this living body and the world, rendering pure subjectivism impossible. On Berendzen's view, this effectively turns Merleau-Ponty into an “anti-subjectivist” who values the facticity of experience, yet still acknowledges the subject's co-creative role in constituting the real.
Berendzen then clarifies Merleau-Ponty's understanding of transcendental subjectivity. Rather than a detached Cartesian “I think,” Merleau-Ponty's subject is inherently situated and cannot be separated from its sensory, embodied existence. He regards the body as the primary site of experience, inherently connected to the world it perceives. Such a view bridges the gap between idealism and realism by affirming that, although the perceiver helps shape meaning, this is always accomplished through material conditions that the body discloses.
Merleau-Ponty's ontology likewise diverges from conventional metaphysical systems, focusing instead on the interplay between subject and environment. Berendzen explains that Merleau-Ponty conceives being as a kind of ongoing movement—a “‘whirling” or shifting exchange from which significance emerges. Traditional Western philosophy often portrays subject and object as distinctly opposed. In contrast, Merleau-Ponty sees their boundaries as permeable, shaped by fluid interactions that neither purely objective nor purely subjective categories can capture. This emphasis on movement and relationality parallels recent discussions of enactivism and embodied cognition.
The role of intersubjectivity also features prominently. Berendzen highlights how Merleau-Ponty's transcendental idealism incorporates the presence of other subjects in a way that counters Cartesian and Kantian isolation. Shared experience shapes and enriches individual perception, embedding the subject in a social horizon. However, this intersubjective framework does not fully escape the bounds of subjective idealism, as Merleau-Ponty continues to ground his philosophy in the self. In other words, even though he introduces intersubjectivity and the socialization of perception, his idealism still remains rooted in the self as the starting point. Therefore, despite adopting the theme of intersubjectivity, Merleau-Ponty's idealism cannot completely transcend its subjective idealist foundation.
Despite the rich analysis Berendzen offers, he focuses primarily on Merleau-Ponty's early work, notably The Structure of Behavior and Phenomenology of Perception. By doing so, he leaves aside later developments in Merleau-Ponty's thought where certain positions evolve, and earlier assumptions undergo more radical questioning. This omission hints at unresolved tensions. For instance, Merleau-Ponty's increasing skepticism toward any neat system of consciousness might challenge the stability of a “transcendental” perspective. The later works arguably suggest that his project cannot be identified with a form of idealism—even a bodily one—without significant qualifications.
A second point of concern revolves around whether a transcendental approach can fully do justice to the deeply pre-reflective and often opaque nature of perception. Merleau-Ponty repeatedly argued that much of our experience is not neatly articulable through conceptual frameworks. Berendzen recognizes this but does not extensively examine how Merleau-Ponty's desire to preserve the primacy of embodied, pre-reflective perception might place limits on any systematic transcendental analysis. The risk, as Merleau-Ponty saw it, was lapsing back into “intellectualism”—the very stance he aimed to dislodge.
Ultimately, Embodied Idealism is a significant addition to Merleau-Ponty scholarship. Berendzen engages in deep analysis and provides outstanding material for any reader interested in phenomenology, idealism, or philosophy of embodiment. However, the unresolved tensions between embodiment and transcendental analysis (and especially the later works) suggest that more could be done to lay out the implications of embodied transcendental idealism. Despite these limitations, the book is worthwhile: It sheds light on the development of Merleau-Ponty's thought and invites readers to probe deeper into his evolving philosophy.
